original_question: (M. Bialy) Assume that a plane billiard has a family of rotational invariant circles with all the rotation numbers in the interval (0, 1/2). Then the billiard table is an ellipse.
target_in_paper: Conjecture 4.9 (M. Bialy) in §4.2.2, “Geometry of caustics, invariant surfaces, and commuting billiard maps.” ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6158379/))
correct_elements: Your draft is essentially the official formulation of Conjecture 4.9: it has the right subject (plane billiard), the right hypothesis (a family of rotational invariant circles with rotation numbers filling (0, 1/2)), the right conclusion (the table is an ellipse), and the correct attribution to M. Bialy. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6158379/))
missing_details: The paper’s billiard setting is a Euclidean plane billiard in a strictly convex domain Ω⊂R^2 bounded by a smooth curve γ; these ambient hypotheses are supplied in §4.2 and are not stated in the draft. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/718695571/1804-03737))

The invariant circles are invariant circles of the billiard map in its phase space (the space of oriented lines / oriented geodesics), not circles drawn inside the table. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/718695571/1804-03737))

For a stand-alone formulation, “has a family ... with all the rotation numbers in (0,1/2)” should be made explicit as: for every ω∈(0,1/2), the billiard map has such an invariant circle with rotation number ω. The paper’s wording suggests that the whole interval is realized. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6158379/))

The conclusion “the billiard table is an ellipse” means that the boundary curve γ of the billiard table is an ellipse. This is implicit from the setup in §4.2. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/718695571/1804-03737))

The nearby context identifies the conjecture as being motivated by Innami’s theorem about a sequence of convex caustics with rotation numbers tending to 1/2; this helps fix the intended scope and shows that the target is not the broader Birkhoff conjecture. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6158379/))

The paper uses the phrase “rotational invariant circles” in the billiard-map context of §4.2.2, but for a stand-alone rewrite one should tie that phrase explicitly to the billiard map and its rotation numbers rather than leave it floating. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6158379/))
refined_question: Let Ω⊂R^2 be a strictly convex planar billiard table with smooth boundary γ, and let T be the associated billiard map on the phase space of oriented lines intersecting γ. Assume that T admits a family of rotational invariant circles whose set of rotation numbers contains the whole interval (0,1/2), equivalently, for every ω∈(0,1/2) there exists a rotational invariant circle of T with rotation number ω. Must γ be an ellipse?
justification: This is the exact target because the draft matches Conjecture 4.9 almost verbatim; the distinctive phrases “rotational invariant circles” and “all the rotation numbers in the interval (0,1/2)” identify that conjecture uniquely, rather than the broader Birkhoff conjecture (Conjecture 4.1) or Kaloshin’s q0-rational integrability conjecture (Conjecture 4.8). The context needed to make it stand-alone comes from §4.2 (definition of the plane billiard, its phase space, and billiard map) and from the immediately preceding paragraph in §4.2.2 (rotation-number language and the motivation via Innami’s theorem); Question 4.10 right after Conjecture 4.9 confirms the intended narrow scope. ([scribd.com](https://www.scribd.com/document/718695571/1804-03737))
